1/9 A withdrawal that sends Ether before clearing the caller balance can be withdrawn against again. The balance is still unchanged when control comes back.
2/9 Calling another contract hands it control. It can call back into the caller before the first call returns, while state is not yet finalized.
3/9 State updates placed after untrusted calls allow repeated execution. That ordering is what makes the callback dangerous.
4/9 Reentrancy is not limited to Ether transfers. It can arise from calls to other contracts, and dependencies across multiple contracts also matter.
5/9 The fix is checks-effects-interactions: validate inputs and permissions, update the relevant storage state, then make external calls.
6/9 In the withdrawal case, save the amount and clear the stored balance with `balances[msg.sender] = 0;` before calling the recipient.
7/9 Then require the call to succeed, so a failure reverts the whole operation.
8/9 A callback may enter through another function or dependency, so review other callable paths and contracts that share the affected state.
9/9 Does any storage write in a function come after a call to another contract, or can a callback reach shared state through a different function?

1/8 A lending protocol that values collateral with a price an attacker can move will make liquidation and borrowing decisions on wrong values. That is price oracle manipulation.
2/8 An oracle is a trust boundary. The contract implicitly trusts that the price reflects market conditions, and manipulation, staleness or misconfiguration can break that trust.
3/8 The protocol trusts price inputs attackers can move. When a price can be influenced directly or indirectly, every decision built on it inherits that weakness.
4/8 OWASP lists several forms: spot price manipulation through large trades, flash loans or just-in-time liquidity in the same block, and TWAP manipulation over short windows or low-liquidity periods.
5/8 Two more forms: stale or stuck data when freshness is not enforced, and aggregation that fails to reject outliers.
6/8 On the input side, aggregate multiple sources with a median or mean and reject outliers. Use TWAPs over sufficient windows and reject prices older than a maximum staleness threshold.
7/8 Avoid basing core prices on illiquid pools, and cap the impact of a single pool or feed. Also halt sensitive operations such as borrowing and liquidations on suspicious or unavailable data.
8/8 Monitor deviations between the oracle and reference markets with automated alerts. Does any borrow or liquidation path read a price with no staleness check and no cap on a single pool or feed?

1/9 A loop that pushes Ether to many recipients needs every payment to succeed. One recipient that fails can block the whole operation for everyone.
2/9 External calls can fail accidentally or deliberately. When progress depends on every call in a batch succeeding, a single failing call stops all the rest.
3/9 The Solidity documentation adds that sending Ether can fail because the recipient runs out of gas, including through require, assert or revert.
4/9 With transfer or send plus a return value check, this can give the recipient a way to block progress in the sending contract.
5/9 Think of payments pushed to many recipients in a loop: the loop only finishes if each recipient accepts its payment. One refusing recipient blocks the rest.
6/9 Isolate each external call into its own transaction that the recipient of the call can initiate. Avoid combining multiple calls in one transaction, especially inside a loop.
7/9 For payments, let users withdraw funds instead of pushing funds to them automatically. This also reduces the chance of problems with the gas limit.
8/9 Always assume external calls can fail, and write the contract logic to handle a failed call. Pull-style withdrawals keep one recipient's failure from blocking others.
9/9 Check your payout code for one condition: does any loop send Ether to a recipient and require that every send succeeds before it can finish?
